samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with George Smerick was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Adam Lehr
sp.p: Hi, I'm Adam Lehr, and this is my two friends.

sp.speaker: Adam Lehr
sp.p: And we will be interviewing Mr. Smerick. Okay.

sp.speaker: George Smerick
sp.p: Now, my name is George -- am I on now? My name is George Smerick. I'm Adam's near neighbor. We've been neighbors for a number of years, and he has a project -- him and his friends have a project, that they want to interview a World War II veteran from his experiences in the military. Anything else? Okay. I'm going to start with my -- I was taken into the Army -- it's on now, huh?

sp.speaker: George Smerick
sp.p: I was taken into the Army when I lived in Western Pennsylvania, and I was taken in 1942, and was sent into training at Camp Campbell, Kentucky, which is now Fort Campbell, Kentucky, which is for paratroopers now, I think. But I was sent into the 12th Armored Division. And wound up as a so-called grunt, and that's an infantry man. I went through training and field -- mostly field training, very little training within the barracks and then we went -- Tennessee maneuvers, which is field training. And then we got sent down to Camp Barkett (ph) of Texas, and we went through training there, working with other armored divisions. I don't know if I mentioned I'm a -- I was in the Armored Division, 12th Armored Division. And I wound up to be an infantryman. But in the period of two years training here in the states before we went overseas, I worked my way up to the rank of Staff Sergeant. And that took over what they call a light machine gun squad. In other words, I had twelve men and used their two machine guns. So after that, we just went over to England. And then from there we were sent over to France, and the war was going on then. This was in November of 1942 -- 1944, I'm sorry. 1942 is when I went in the service -- but when I when I went into France, we got prepared to go into combat. We moved up closer to the front and then in December, when we went into the battlefront, that was what happened. I'm sure you're too young to know about the Battle of Bulge. Did you hear the Battle of the Bulge in World War II? Okay. The Germans attacked the American line -- defense line, and they wanted to capture Belgium and get to the coast. Well, they didn't make it. We went into combat the 3rd of December 1944, and then the 16th of December, we were up in the frontlines. Now, 16th of December, the Germans decided they were going to push our troops into the ocean or into the channel -- English Channel, but they didn't get too far. We were in combat with the Germans -- oh, from the 16th of January -- well, from the 3rd of December - 16th of January. We fought against them in the Bulge, but then toward the 1st of the year, right after Christmas -- we were on the frontlines in Christmas time -- and after we kind of held the Germans back and started pushing them back, then they took us away from there and sent us farther south. Now, this area is called the Ardennes Forest. Anyhow, this was called the Ardennes Forest, and we got out of there and sent us down to an area around Strassburg, which is in Alsace Lorraine, which is still not France and it's not Germany but it's a mixture of people -- a mixture of Germans and mixture of French. So my division -- we were put in what they call reserve. We were held back in case the division needed help. Well, the division got into a fight in a small town called Herxheim, and they got beat up pretty bad. They lost a lot of tanks; they lost a lot of men. One time they would -- for maybe a day or two, they would be beating the daylights out of the Germans and capturing them by the thousands, and then the Germans would turn around and come back and they'd start another attack, and they got beat up pretty bad. Finally, we got orders to give them relief, but we were sent into what is called a suicide mission. In other words, we had no idea how many Germans were there -- we would attack -- how many were there -- we'd have to fight them and they didn't give us -- my unit did not give any help to us. In other words, they didn't give us no mortar fire, any artillery. They didn't give us any small arms fire. They just sent us in there. And when we come up close to their lines, at 4 o'clock in the morning, we come to the their lines, our scout -- that's the guy who goes out ahead -- You're still working on it? Okay. -- The guy that goes out ahead to see what's out there. He captured two outposts, German soldiers, and they said to get out of there because it's loaded with German soldiers and they were dug in, and they had all kinds of weapons and everything. But our Lieutenant, who was running the company, he said, "No. My orders are to attack." Well then all of the sudden, I heard a boom, and the flares was just coming down like -- like sparks from a -- stars coming down. They were flares on parachutes. As they came down real slow, they lit that whole area up where we were. And it lit it up so bright, it was like daylight, and they were shooting our -- their machine guns and sending in mortar fire artillery and rifle fire, sniper fire, and a lot of the men were getting wounded and killed. They were screaming for medics, hollering, "Medic, I'm wounded." They were -- well, naturally, being wounded you're scared, you know. So they were asking for their mothers. They were asking for their wives. They were asking for their girlfriends. And I was laying in front of another soldier, and he was laying still so I figured he got killed. He was -- or badly wounded. Off to my left, as far as you can look over there to my wife sitting in the chair, lay another one of my soldiers and he was hollering for me, "Sergeant Smerick, please shoot me. I can't stand the pain." I said, "I can't do that, just wait. We're going to get help." But he died. He died right there. I couldn't help him. And shooting him wouldn't help. It was against my -- against anything, you know. So after laying there for -- oh, approximately eight hours -- we laid in -- the field we were laying on was part marsh that had been frozen over and part land. There was nothing to hide behind, no trees, no shrubbery. But I must have been laying in the low spot or the boy in front of me that got killed must have took the bullet meant for me. I don't know. Only the good Lord knows that. But after they kept begging us -- the Germans kept hollering out to please surrender. We'll take care of your wounded. And finally between myself with that rank up there and -- I didn't have that rank at that time, I was just one stripe below. I was a Staff Sergeant. Between me and the other high ranking Staff Sergeant -- he was in the service longer than me -- we decided it's best. Now's the time to help our wounded. We're not going to get any help. It's about 2 o'clock in the afternoon, and the sun is just barely coming through a hazy fog like -- so we decided to surrender and take care of our wounded, which we did. I did all I could to help the -- one I remember is one of my good friends. The machine gun bullets hit him in his shoulder, and his arm was just hanging from the gristle or bone -- shattered bone from machine gun bullets. So I helped him and a German medic helped. And another one, his knee was shot off. All this part of his knee -- kneecap -- and he couldn't walk. We couldn't carry him. We couldn't do nothing with him. So we dragged him -- would you believe -- on his back, grabbed a hold of his hands, and dragged him backwards to the German aid soldier? And then they put him on some kind of a carrier and took him to the German aid station, which is a cement building like they used -- how would I say it? In defense. So that's where they had the medics in there. I saw some very, very terrible sights of wounded men. Even German soldiers that were wounded were brought into that medical aid station. The worst I saw was the tanker. They brought him in, and he had no face. He was burnt. The tank caught on fire. We watched the tank get hit with one of our tanks, hit with a 75 millimeter shell. And when he come out, he practically crawled across the road. And then they got -- the German soldiers went and got him and took him to the aid station. And when he came there, his upper lip was hanging down over his lower lip, you could see his teeth. His eyeballs were hanging out here. His face looked like -- you know what a lake looks like when it's dry? It's all cracked. That's what his face looked like, and it was black. The fluid and the blood was seeping out through there, so they took him down into that building and we heard one shot -- one shot from a pistol. They had to kill him. That's what they call a mercy killing because he couldn't live. He would die a horrible death, so the Germans were different than we -- when it came to their soldiers, if it looked like they couldn't take care of them, they eliminated -- by -- they had -- they carried a 25 caliber revolver, and that's something that we never -- our people never carried a weapon. Our medics did not carry a weapon. But the Germans figured if I can't take care of him, I can't give him any medicine, I can't make him better, boom. Kill him. Now after that was the first -- us and the wounded -- Is it all ready to keep on going? Okay. They put all the wounded on a hey wagon. Now, I know you've probably seen around the farms -- you've seen a flat bed wagon, maybe a horse pulling these Amish people. And we pushed it -- there's no horse to pull it, we had to push it to a farm barn and took off the wounded and then we marched to the Rhine River. They put us on a -- Stop it for a minute. That's better. Now you got it going. They put us on a raft, and took us across the Rhine River and marched us to a prison camp, and they had a brand new camp with brand new wire, brand new wood. And they gave us -- you've seen a milk can, haven't you? About two feet high. Well, they brought in a whole milk can with a big ladle and gave each one of us a tin -- a tin soup thing, or whatever you want to call it, like a tin dish is what they gave us. So they put me in charge, and I had to line everybody up, you know, and make sure everybody got a fair share. And I got the ladle and got the soup and poured it in. But it was pretty thin. Boy, it's pretty thin soup. Here after I fed everybody, I found out that all the solids are in the bottom, like they were kind of vegetables, like -- I can't think of offhand, but different kinds of vegetable are in the bottom. So they start screaming, "I didn't get no thick stuff. I didn't get no thick stuff," you know. But you wonder -- here's men -- some of them still wounded and unable to walk -- and they were fighting about a spoonful of soup. Anyhow, I said, "Okay. Now everybody's going to go back and we're going to give each one another ladle of heavy stuff." So the next day they marched us out of there, and we went to a what they called a railhead, that's where the railroad come in, and they put us onboard what they called forty and eight boxcars. The reason they were called forty and eight, they came from World War I, when they used forty men to transport forty soldiers or eight horses. And they put us in that boxcar, like, locked us in. We had no way of eliminating, you know, having bowel movements or urinating or anything. It was so many of us in there that -- this is the box car. When this side here was standing up, this side laid down. And after a while, somebody would say hey it's about time we switch and all these was laying down would stand, these standing up would lay down, and we'd use one corner of the boxcar to eliminate our whatever he had to do, urinate or whatever. So it was pretty nasty. They give us -- we've got no food, other than that bowl of soup or that dish of soup, that's all the food we had. Oh, I don't know how many days maybe five -- maybe two or three. At night time, the train would go and it would sit there for hours at a railhead somewhere, and they wouldn't go anywhere then, because they were afraid to move their train with prisoners on it that would block their troop movements. So they got us -- finally, after about five days and about three nights, we got to Ludwisburg, Germany, which is near Stuttgart and they put us in prison camp there. And you'd be surprised what we were put into. Now, you know what a horse stable looks like. You've seen horse stables. You know they're nice, nice -- strong, and nice new wood and everything. Well, when we went in this building, it was a horse stable. But the Germans believed very highly on horses, so they build a building made out of brick and the stalls were put inside that building and in the center -- like this is the whole building inside -- this is all brick -- beautiful building, real nice building. And in the middle was a trough -- a water trough. But there was no water in there for us, and we had to lay on the floor. There was no kind of bedding, no kind of beds. We had to -- I don't know how long we stayed there. Oh, this is a good one. He said you had to shave. Well, you see I need a shave right now, and I'm letting that go for a reason. But anyhow, they said you have to shave. So the guys -- they were prisoners there -- and they were, like, in charge. They gave each man -- they had us lined up -- take a soap, a razor with a double edge razor blade in it, and that soup dish. Now, this -- you have to go outside there and catch water off of the roof that's dripping down from the snow and ice. Remember now, it's winter time, and the ice -- the water would be ice cold. And yet, how do you shave with ice cold water? And just take a soap, and I rubbed it on there and I'll tell you it felt like they were pulling them whiskers out one at a time. It hurt that bad. And anyhow, each one of us had a good shave. We shaved -- I think it was 21 days of a beard that I had on my face, I assume. Everybody else had that much beard, too. So then they moved us from there and put us back in boxcars again and there we were another three -- four -- five days a couple of nights and we wound up in a place called Hammelburg, which is between Frankfurt and Schweinfurt. Schweinfurt was a very industrial city and our American planes -- we could look out and watch them come in thousands of them -- thousands. They'd leave them vapor trails -- you see vapor trails here? -- and those vapor trails would be behind them. These were B17 bombers. They were going over to Frankfurt and over to Schweinfurt bombing. Well now, here's another thing, when we got to Hammelburg, we had to climb a stone road up a side of a mountain. We could look back in the valley where the train left us off -- down the train head -- the railhead, and it's beautiful. It's such a beautiful valley down there, like you see on TV, and when we got to the top, they put us in another one of those horse stables. And there was -- it was so crowded the downstairs part where the horses would normally be was so crowded there was no room for us to -- my group -- I don't know how many of us there were. They made us go to the second floor which had a hey mound, but you wouldn't believe that their hey mound had hardwood floors like you have in your house. That's hard to believe, but that's what they had. That's how well they treated their horses, but they didn't treat us that way. We got no beds, no kind of -- what they did give us was a gunnysack or potato sack with wood shavings in it, and that's what our mattress was. So four of us would lay together spoon fashion. In other words, back to back -- back to belly or whatever until, you know, we'd get sore from laying and it hurts on the hip. We'd have to turn over. Well, that lasted until 27th of March. One day, we heard our fire. Gun fire. And there was a water tower up above our area, and the bullets were flying off that water tower. And here the American GIs come in the camp, chased the Germans out. And I have a story on that by the man that lead that group that come in there. He was ordered by General Patton -- now, you've heard of General Patton, I would think -- he was little on the nasty side, but he was a good soldier. Anyhow, he sent a task force in there to liberate us and that was 50 miles from Frankfurt. And for that day at 4 o'clock in the afternoon, all that evening, all that night until 4 o'clock the next morning, we were liberated but we were too weak to escape. There was no way for us to -- some guys did. Some were strong enough and they tried to get away by going in the woods, but they were eventually captured -- recaptured. Anyhow, talking about the food that we were getting, it was a bowl of that soup, all kinds of stuff in it. It had rutabagas, it had beet leaves, it had oak leaves, it had -- you think of it -- and a piece of black bread, they called it. We called it black bread. Would you hit your button there? Shut it off. Shut it off. Okay. Now we're back to -- I can't find the -- how will I say it? -- the recipe for that bread they gave us. Some days we'd get two slices of bread; other days we'd get maybe half of half a loaf per man, but it was made mainly of sawdust and a few other grains that the Germans had, like rye and stuff like that. And that's what the bread was made out of. The liquid they gave us was what we called ersatz tea or coffee. It was made -- we called it burnt barley tea because they would roast the barley and then make -- like, grind it and make it like a coffee. That was the first thing in the morning they would give us that. Then about 1 or 2 o'clock in the afternoon they would give us a bowl of soup. They'd come down into the compound, open up the gate and bring in this wagon with two great big barrels on it, and a couple of GIs POWs would be on there with a big dipper. And he would dip down into that big barrel and come up with this soup made out of, like I said, all kinds of barley and sometimes potatoes -- mostly garbage that you would throw away. You wouldn't feed it to human beings. It was pig food is what it was. And my assistant squad leader found in his bowl of soup one day a little chunk of bone about as big as my thumb, and he showed it to me and he kept that as a souvenir. Here it was the part of a jawbone of a horse. That's what they made the soup out of. They'd use -- cut the meat off a horse -- a dead horse, and they would cut the meat off the horse's head and whatever meat was on the bones they would make this soup. That's what we had. Oh, where do I go from here? Shut it off. Okay. After I said we were liberated for them -- those twelve hours they got scared and they took us down in the mountain and put us on a train -- those forty eight cars, and we went down it took about three days and a couple of nights to go down to Nuremberg. Now, if you study your history of Germany, Nuremberg was the capital, sort of, of the German regime, you know, the government. And so we arrived there early in the -- we arrived there during the night this camp, and we couldn't see cause it was still dark, but when it got daylight, they opened up the doors, and we practically fell out. We were so crowded in there, you know, pushed up against each other in threes that when we got out on the ground, we couldn't believe what we were looking at. There was air corps Prisoners of War who were playing ball. They were playing ball with gloves, baseballs, bats. They had a small field, and they were playing ball out there. And they had barracks to live in. Their mess hall -- mess hall is a place where you eat, you know, like a restaurant -- and they had dishes, nice white dishes they get to eat their food on. We couldn't believe this. But when they saw us, that's the first they did -- stopped everything and ran over and help us get into a big tent. They had a big tent there, like a circus tent, and they put us in there and the first they did -- throughout the war, they had what was called the Red Cross box. Now, those boxes came from all over the world and allies like Australia, New Zealand, England, France, Spain, United States. In that box there would be food, canned powdered milk, a can of -- people hate spam today but oh, we loved it. But we had to cut it into little pieces to give it to each guy. They'd give you one box and say eight men have to eat from this for a week. Yeah. So then we found out later, lets see -- oh, from -- from Nuremberg, they told us we're going to march. We're going to march to Austria. That's down over Southeastern Germany, across the Danube River. All those famous places you hear about now, I saw them as a Prisoner of War, but I didn't enjoy it, believe me. Anyhow, we marched. They gave us one meal in fourteen days. And that was a real thick pea soup. You could hardly swallow it, it was so thick. But then after that International Red Cross come up from Switzerland in a truck, and it was about fourteen days. I think they gave us to spread among like four men a Red Cross box. So we wouldn't starve. We were starving, you know. You put a message on there that you had it switched.

sp.speaker: Adam Lehr
sp.p: Okay. The tape was switched around we will begin where he left off before. So --

sp.speaker: George Smerick
sp.p: That sounds pretty good. Now, I was talking about this big circus tent. This tent was as big as this whole property from this Hoffman Avenue over to Main Street from Spruce Street up to your place. That's how big this tent was. And they put us all in there. And by the time we got there, there was no place to lay down, no place to -- and you know what was on the floor? Rocks. As big as tennis balls. That's what they had for a floor. We had to lay on that. We still had our GI clothes on, you know, our battle clothes. I was lucky. I had a tanker suit which was insulated and real nice and thick. But four of us would lay together, would lay facing one direction with our back to somebody's front and then would get something hurt -- maybe a rock was hitting somebody's bone, and we'd have to switch over. Well, that was Moosburg camp 7A; they called it B11 which is Roman numeral for seven. And then one day, they said that -- we could hear tanks. Tanks are noisy. Boy, they're noisy. At least they were then. Anyhow, we could hear the tanks about 50 miles away -- not tanks, artillery. And the tanks were 10 miles away. General Patton was coming in there to liberate the camp. He was coming in with the 10th Armored Divisions. I don't how much other soldiers he had. But I saw him personally, as close as I am to you here. He said -- he was pretty mouthy, you know, he used pretty foul language -- but he says I'll get these Bs -- bastards, you know. I'll get these -- I'll make them pay for this. And then we waited five days and five nights before they put us on a truck and took us to Regensburg where there's an air field, and they were bringing -- they were still fighting the war now. They were still going toward Austria -- toward Eastern Germany, and when we got off the trucks up there at Regensburg. There we saw these planes coming, one after another, just like B17 bombers, only they were C47 cargo planes and they were bringing in gasoline -- five gallon cans inside those planes. And they would land. They would shut their engines off -- they had two engines, and they would unload the gasoline. Now, you can imagine what that smelled like to a GI -- a POW that's sick, you know -- oh, we were puking and everything. We stole food off the trucks. They had D rations, K rations, C rations. We just gobbled all that food up. That's crazy, but that's what we did. We didn't know any better. And as soon as that gasoline was off, on the plane 25 men, closed the door, took off. Well, I think we all got sick before we got up there and leveled off, puking all over the place, and then we went to sleep because we hadn't slept much more than a couple hours in five days -- five nights. So as we were going over the Rhine valley -- the Rhine River Valley, everybody was on the floor in that slop, in our puke, you know. What happened? And the air corps guy -- I don't know what his job was, but I think I know. But I can't think of it now. Anyhow, he came back and says everybody okay? Oh, yeah. We're all right. We're just puking all over the place. So he said, well, what happened? He says we hit an air pocket and we dropped 500 feet like that, just boom -- right down. But then we got air again and went back up to 5000 feet, and they said there's a Camp Lucky Strike. First thing to do is take off them filthy dirty clothes you got. We had them on for six months. I only had a couple of showers all the time I was in combat and a Prisoner of War. Anyhow, to finish it up now -- to finish it up and maybe you'll want to ask some questions or make a statement while it's still running. They made us take all them clothes off, kept what personal things we wanted to keep and they put it in a -- like a netted bag and hung it up. And we went in there, and I showered for one whole hour. One whole hour. The bottom of my feet was a quarter inch of scum. You know we didn't bathe -- stunk. Oh man, I don't know how we lived with each other, but everybody smelled the same. So what are you going to do? So I -- like I said -- and we used -- you know what a course scrub brush is? That's what I used on my body -- elbows, knees, bottom of my feet, the privates. And like I said, I spent a whole hour, and in that shower -- and when I come back out stark naked, go down the line there and you get your new clothes. They give us all nice, new clothes, underwear (inaudible) everything, new shoes, everything. That was the end of it, and then we finally were sent back to the states. So you want to stop it now and think of -- His question was how long was I a Prisoner of War and that question is always asked, how long. Well, when you're suffering and when you're starving, time doesn't mean too much. So whether you were a prisoner for two months, four months, or a year, it really doesn't count. It's how you survived the experience that you went through as a POW. There was something else there I wanted to -- Well that's about -- anybody else? Leave it running.

sp.speaker: Adam Lehr
sp.p: Okay. How did you feel about the war?

sp.speaker: George Smerick
sp.p: How did I feel about World War II? Well, I'm a little bitter, simply because they sent us on this -- as far as the being in the war and coming close to death, I was bitter because they sent us in on this suicide mission for -- didn't accomplish nothing. We didn't gain nothing by going in there and having my whole company -- 67 percent of my company of men, or roughly 120, went into combat that day. We accomplished nothing. We just -- the division lost a half a company just like that. In the army, you're expendable, like a tent pin. In other words, you -- they don't care whether you live or die when you're in combat. But tent pins was always a thing we used because tent pins -- if you lost it, you'd get another one for nothing, but it you lost something else like half of your pup tent, then you got charged for it. But a tent pin? Throw them away any time. So that's -- I'm a little bitter there, and I have to be. As far as the rest of my military experience, when I was being interrogated, he was trying to get me to admit what unit I was with -- that's typical. But all you had to give was your name, rank, and serial number and I kept saying that. My name is George E. Smerick. My rank is Staff Sergeant. My serial number is 33393692. That's my number, I remembered 60 years ago. Anyhow, he didn't like the answers I was giving, you were with this unit. I don't know, you said I was with that unit. And I seen his eyes flicker over to a soldier standing there with a rifle down to the ground -- had his butt down to the ground, and on the end he had his bayonet -- and their bayonet is different from ours. It's like a rod sharpened with a real pointy -- about as long as that paper. He picked up the rifle and came at me and I went like this -- I didn't get a Purple Heart for this -- you see. Can you see that scar?

sp.speaker: George Smerick
sp.p: I was bayoneted there, but cause no one saw it, I can't get a Purple Heart. Then when he got angry at me for not answering questions, this time he come at me with that gun -- that bayonet. He hit my glasses -- my GI glasses. I didn't have these kind, the Army gave me glasses -- hit them glasses and hit me right there above my eyebrow, and you can see it. It just cut straight to the bone, see? So I got two Purple Hearts, and I can't get them. I don't care. They want to keep them? Let them bury them. If I try to get through ex-POW with -- how are you going to get it when nobody's there? Each one of us were interrogated individually, and they won't accept that. That no one was there. We had no officer. Our officer was killed. We only had one officer. So -- you still recording?

sp.speaker: George Smerick
sp.p: I think we can shut her down for a little while.
